raw_response.adversarial_critique: Claude's stored point estimates, standard errors, and analytic sample size (amc_com OR = 0.60*, SE = 0.14; ngo_com OR = 0.56*, SE = 0.13; areawealth OR = 0.07**, SE = 0.06; distance OR = 1.44*, SE = 0.21; N = 277) match Table 6's water-complaints logistic regression precisely (PDF p. 13 / p. 702), and converting OR < 1 on a complaint outcome into a negative raw log-odds sign (-) and Favourable direction is internally consistent. However, the Favourable verdict selectively extracts external institutional redress contact while omitting the paper's focal internal participation variable—sustained CBO meeting attendance (attend)—which is statistically null and leans toward more complaints in the water model (OR = 1.44, SE = 0.28) and failed bivariate significance screening (—) in the sewerage model (Table 6, p. 702), alongside null NGO decision dominance (d_ngo OR = 0.86, SE = 0.46) and bivariate-excluded CBO activity (active3). Furthermore, Table 6 reports a co-primary sanitation specification (Respondent complains about sewerage, N = 300) in which NGO contact remains favorable (ngo_com OR = 0.50**, SE = 0.13), whereas municipal contact—half of Claude's bundled exposure—is opposite-signed and statistically null (amc_com OR = 1.56, SE = 0.42), and binary municipal contact increases street-lighting complaints (amccntct OR = 8.33*, SE = 6.94). Outcome directness is also only an indirect proxy: all 38 sampled neighbourhoods had already received SNP household water and sewerage connections at least three years prior (PDF p. 8 / p. 697), and the dependent variable only captures whether surveyed CBO leaders/members volunteered an open-ended negative comment about water quality or quantity (20.7%, Table 4, p. 700), which the authors explicitly note may reflect social desirability and complaining outlets rather than objective service quality (PDF p. 10 / p. 699). Finally, Claude's narrative fields mischaracterize amc_com and ngo_com as binary household contact rather than 3-level ordinal frequencies of CBO-level institutional contact (Table 5, p. 701), and the dossier's adjustment list mistakenly includes density, gender, and language (excluded from the water model) while omitting d_ngo and ngo_evl2 (OR = 0.15*, SE = 0.11).

raw_response.numerical_check_note: All 8 numerical estimates and standard errors in estimate_full (amc_com OR = 0.60*, SE = 0.14; ngo_com OR = 0.56*, SE = 0.13; areawealth OR = 0.07**, SE = 0.06; distance OR = 1.44*, SE = 0.21) and the analytic sample size (N = 277) exactly match the 'Respondent complains about water' logistic regression column in Table 6 (PDF p. 13 / journal p. 702). Two non-numerical metadata inaccuracies appear in Claude's text fields: (1) amc_com and ngo_com are 3-level ordinal variables (1 = Never, 2 = Sometimes, 3 = Regularly) measuring how frequently the respondent's CBO approached the municipality or sponsoring NGO in the last 12 months (surveyed among CBO leaders/members; Table 5, p. 701), not binary household-level contact vs. no contact; and (2) the dossier's Adjusted field lists project density, gender, and language (which were omitted via bivariate screening in the water model, marked '—') while omitting d_ngo (OR = 0.86, SE = 0.46) and ngo_evl2 (OR = 0.15*, SE = 0.11), which were included in the 7-df water regression (LR chi2(7) = 49.01).
raw_response.polarity_or_orientation_issue: Table 6 prints Odds Ratios rather than log-odds coefficients and switches outcome polarity between Model 1 (overall SNP quality 'Very Satisfactory', higher = better) and Models 2–4 (open-ended service complaints, higher = worse). For the extracted water-complaint ORs (0.60* and 0.56*), Claude properly converted OR < 1 to negative log-odds (-) and inverted complaint polarity ('higher = worse') to code 'Favourable'. However, treating non-complaining in an open-ended survey prompt as better water access is substantively ambiguous: the authors warn (pp. 699–700) that absence of negative survey comments can reflect social desirability or prior access to external complaining channels rather than superior physical water delivery (and in the street-lighting model, municipal contact amccntct increases complaints, OR = 8.33*). Exposure wording also conflates ordinal CBO-level contact frequency (1–3) with binary household contact.
